note: One paragraph per relation, written from the abstracts of the cited papers (arXiv metadata and Crossref checked 2026-10-06). Each claim about a result is attributed to the paper it comes from. Digitized or compared curves in sim-highline carry their own definitions; this text is context, not evidence.

gsmf.title: Stellar mass function
gsmf.paragraph: The galaxy stellar mass function counts galaxies per unit volume per dex of stellar mass and is the most basic census of how baryons have been turned into stars. Locally it is well described by a double Schechter function with a knee near 10^10.7 M☉ and an upturn at low mass (Baldry et al. 2012, building on earlier SDSS and 2MASS work such as Bell et al. 2003); deep surveys now trace it smoothly to z≈7.5, with the quiescent fraction and the cosmic stellar mass density evolving along with it (Weaver et al. 2023; Madau & Dickinson 2014 review the matching star-formation history). Simulations are usually tuned to it: EAGLE's feedback was calibrated to the z≈0 function and the model then tracks the observed evolution to z=7 within plausible observational uncertainty (Furlong et al. 2015), so agreement near z=0 is a calibration check, not a prediction. The informative tests are the low-mass slope (supernova feedback and resolution), the massive tail (AGN feedback, and how the mass of a central galaxy is defined: the diffuse-light fraction depends sensitively on aperture, Pillepich et al. 2018) and z>4, where JWST now constrains it. Check h-scalings, IMF and mass aperture before reading offsets as physics.

sfms.title: Star-forming main sequence
sfms.paragraph: The star-forming main sequence is the tight, nearly power-law correlation between star-formation rate and stellar mass among star-forming galaxies, and the observational backbone for how fast galaxies grow. Early surveys showed that it exists, that it sits at higher SFR at earlier times, and that star formation in most galaxies declines gradually after an initial onset (Noeske et al. 2007). Putting 25 studies on a common calibration, Speagle et al. (2014) found a consensus of about 0.1 dex between publications, an intrinsic width near 0.2 dex that does not change with cosmic time, and a slope that steepens toward early times; the most recent census to z≈6 finds curvature at high mass whose turnover mass tracks the halo mass at which accretion switches from cold to hot (Popesso et al. 2023). Simulations broadly reproduce the shape and scatter but disagree on normalisation at cosmic noon: Illustris matched z=0 and z=4 yet sat well below the data near z≈2 (Sparre et al. 2015); EAGLE's star-forming galaxies lie 0.2 to 0.4 dex below observed sSFRs while their evolution tracks the data (Furlong et al. 2015); for TNG the answer depends on the star-forming selection, the SFR timescale and the aperture (Donnari et al. 2019). Those systematics are as large as the offsets, so compare definitions before quoting a tension.

ssfr.title: Specific SFR
ssfr.paragraph: Specific star-formation rate, the SFR per unit stellar mass, is the inverse of a galaxy's mass-doubling time and is the main sequence viewed as a ratio. Observationally the sSFR of star-forming galaxies is close to constant with mass below a turnover mass and suppressed above it, and its normalisation rises steeply toward high redshift (Speagle et al. 2014; Popesso et al. 2023); the history this implies is a gradual decline rather than repeated bursts for most galaxies (Noeske et al. 2007), set against a cosmic SFR density that peaked near z≈2 (Madau & Dickinson 2014). In simulations sSFR is one of the least consistent outputs: EAGLE star-forming galaxies are 0.2 to 0.4 dex below observed values at fixed mass (Furlong et al. 2015), Illustris is too low near z≈2 (Sparre et al. 2015), and TNG values move by a comparable amount with the SFR timescale and aperture (Donnari et al. 2019). Physically, sSFR tracks the gas supply relative to the existing stars, so an offset points to gas accretion, gas fractions or feedback, but observed values also depend on the SFR indicator, the SED model and the IMF, which are not always converted. A threshold in sSFR is also what separates star-forming from quenched galaxies in many codes, which links sSFR tensions to quenched-fraction tensions.

mzr.title: Gas-phase mass–metallicity relation
mzr.paragraph: The mass–metallicity relation links a galaxy's stellar mass to the oxygen abundance of its star-forming gas. In about 53,000 SDSS galaxies it is tight (±0.1 dex), steep from 10^8.5 to 10^10.5 M☉ and flat above, which Tremonti et al. (2004) read as evidence that galactic winds remove metals most effectively from low-mass galaxies; at fixed mass it also depends on SFR (the fundamental metallicity relation, revisited on a Te-anchored scale by Curti et al. 2020). The absolute abundance scale is still uncertain: Te-based calibrations give a significantly lower normalisation than photoionisation-model ones (Curti et al. 2020), and the review by Maiolino & Mannucci (2019) lays out how the relation evolves with redshift and how it compares with models and simulations. IllustrisTNG reproduces the slope and the normalisation evolution at 0<z<2 over 10^9 to 10^10.5 M☉ and predicts a gradual decline at higher redshift (about −0.064 dex per unit z); the evolution is driven mainly by higher gas fractions, not by changes in metal retention, and most metals at z=0 lie outside the ISM (Torrey et al. 2019). FIRE zoom simulations also agree reasonably with the observed relation at z=0 to 3 and predict its evolution to z=6 in terms of gas and stellar mass fractions (Ma et al. 2016). Simulations report different tracers (O/H, Z/Z☉, metal mass fraction) and different gas selections, so sim-highline keeps them on separate axes and never mixes them.

zstar.title: Stellar mass–stellar metallicity relation
zstar.paragraph: The stellar mass–stellar metallicity relation traces the time-integrated enrichment of a galaxy's stars, so it responds more slowly than the gas-phase relation to recent accretion and outflows. From SDSS spectra, Gallazzi et al. (2005) found low-mass galaxies young and metal-poor and massive galaxies old and metal-rich, with a rapid change at intermediate mass; resolved-star spectroscopy shows that dwarf irregulars and dwarf spheroidals follow one relation, Z★ ∝ M★^0.30, roughly continuous with galaxies up to 10^12 M☉ (Kirby et al. 2013). The chemical-evolution review of Maiolino & Mannucci (2019) stresses that stellar and gas-phase metallicities carry complementary information and compares both with simulations. Simulations predict the same positive trend: FIRE zoom simulations agree reasonably with the observed relations at z=0 to 3 and predict stellar metallicity rising with mass with a slope near 0.40 and a normalisation that declines with redshift, linked to the evolution of stellar and gas mass fractions (Ma et al. 2016). Absolute values nevertheless depend on the assumed yields, on whether metallicity is mass- or light-weighted, on the aperture and on the adopted solar abundance, which in this data well ranges from 0.0127 to 0.0142, so slope and evolution are safer comparisons than normalisation. Observational values come from a mix of absorption-line indices and full spectral fitting with different age–metallicity degeneracies.

size.title: Mass–size relation
size.paragraph: The size–mass relation says that more massive galaxies are larger, with different slopes and zero points for star-forming and quiescent systems. SDSS showed that late-type sizes scale as M^0.15 below about 10^10.6 M☉ and as M^0.4 above, with early types steeper at M^0.55 (Shen et al. 2003); HST surveys then established that quiescent galaxies were much more compact at high redshift, with R_eff ∝ (1+z)^−1.48 against (1+z)^−0.75 for star-forming galaxies (van der Wel et al. 2014), and that the median size of the most massive galaxies keeps evolving out to z≈3 (Mowla et al. 2019); Conselice (2014) reviews the structural evolution behind this. EAGLE agrees with observations to about 0.1 dex at z<1 and 0.2 to 0.3 dex at 1<z<2, with passive galaxies smaller than active ones at fixed mass (Furlong et al. 2017); TNG100 reproduces the trends and matches projected r-band sizes within 0.25 dex over 0<z<2, and shows quenched galaxies hardly growing in size before they quench while main-sequence galaxies grow steadily (Genel et al. 2018). Size growth therefore records accretion of angular momentum, mergers and the timing of quenching. Beware the definition: 3D half-mass radii and projected half-light radii (which depend on wavelength) differ by tenths of a dex, and sim-highline refuses to score one against the other.

refs.cite: van der Wel et al. 2014, ApJ 788, 28

shmr.title: Stellar–halo mass relation
shmr.paragraph: The stellar-to-halo mass relation measures how efficiently halos have converted baryons into stars. Abundance matching and its descendants (Behroozi et al. 2013; Moster et al. 2013) found a relation sharply peaked near halo masses of 10^12 M☉ that changes with redshift; the review by Wechsler & Tinker (2018) concludes that galaxy-formation efficiency is a strong function of halo mass and that the galaxy–halo connection is both a key test of galaxy formation models and an input to cosmological constraints. UniverseMachine ties galaxy growth to halo assembly and finds that quenching at z>1 correlates strongly with halo mass (Behroozi et al. 2019). At the massive end the observations themselves are uncertain: brightest-cluster-galaxy stellar masses scale as M500^0.35, and earlier abundance-matching results underestimated them by factors of 2 to 4 because the photometry missed outer light (Kravtsov et al. 2018). Simulations are partly calibrated to the relation and then differ in detail: in TNG the 3D stellar mass within 30 kpc scales as M500c^0.49 with 0.12 dex scatter, and the diffuse-light fraction depends strongly on how a central galaxy's mass is defined (Pillepich et al. 2018). The halo-mass definition (M200c, Bryan–Norman virial, FOF) and the stellar aperture each shift curves by amounts that rival differences between models.

bh.title: Black hole–stellar mass relation
bh.paragraph: The black hole–stellar mass relation connects the mass of a galaxy's central black hole to the total stellar mass of its host, and is the main constraint on how black holes grow relative to their galaxies. Dynamical masses show that black holes correlate with bulges but weakly with disks and halos, which Kormendy & Ho (2013) take as evidence against simple coevolution; broad-line AGN samples extend the relation to lower-mass hosts (Reines & Volonteri 2015), and searches for intermediate-mass black holes suggest that many 10^9 to 10^10 M☉ galaxies host black holes below 10^5 M☉, with the relation continuing at large scatter (Greene et al. 2020). Simulations differ strongly in black-hole seeding and in their supernova and AGN feedback. Habouzit et al. (2021) compare Illustris, TNG100, TNG300, Horizon-AGN, EAGLE and SIMBA and find that all produce tight relations but struggle to make black holes below 10^7.5 M☉ in galaxies of 10^10.5 to 10^11.5 M☉, that the mean relation evolves mildly (under 1 dex in black-hole mass for 0<z<5) with code-dependent shape and normalisation, and that supernova feedback strength shapes the relation below 10^10.5 M☉. Observed samples are subject to selection effects (resolving the sphere of influence, AGN luminosity), so compare like with like.

bhsigma.title: Black hole–velocity dispersion (M–σ)
bhsigma.paragraph: The M–σ relation links black-hole mass to the stellar velocity dispersion of the host bulge, and is the tightest of the black-hole scaling relations. Two groups established it in 2000 with slopes that did not initially agree (M ∝ σ^4.8 for Ferrarese & Merritt 2000; M ∝ σ^3.75 with 0.30 dex scatter for Gebhardt et al. 2000). The review by Kormendy & Ho (2013) places it in a picture where black holes correlate best with bulge properties; van den Bosch (2016) finds M ∝ σ^5.4 and shows the relation is an edge-on view of a plane involving black-hole mass, galaxy mass and size; and at the low-mass end it appears to continue unbroken to about 10^5 M☉ with large scatter (Greene et al. 2020). Simulations rarely compute σ the way observers measure it, so comparisons depend on the aperture, weighting and projection used, and several codes were calibrated to a black-hole–bulge or black-hole–stellar mass relation rather than to M–σ (Habouzit et al. 2021). Physically, a tight M–σ is read as regulation of black-hole growth by the depth of the central potential, but selection effects and the unresolved sphere of influence matter for both data and models. sim-highline stores the dispersion definition per record and refuses to rank across different ones.

jstar.title: Stellar specific angular momentum–mass relation
jstar.paragraph: The specific angular momentum–mass relation, the Fall relation, ties the angular momentum per unit mass of a galaxy's stars to its stellar mass. In ΛCDM, tidal torques give halos j ∝ M^(2/3), so disks that retain their angular momentum should follow that slope; observations show parallel tracks for ellipticals and spirals, with ellipticals holding about 3 to 4 times less (Romanowsky & Fall 2012), and the SPARC rotation-curve sample now defines the relation for spirals over 10^7 to 10^11.5 M☉ (Posti et al. 2018). Simulations reproduce the broad picture: Illustris galaxies fall on two relations, with late types retaining essentially all the angular momentum from cosmological torques and early types about 30% (Genel et al. 2015); Magneticum disk and spheroid galaxies compare well with observations (Teklu et al. 2015); and EAGLE agrees at z=0, with a scatter that correlates with morphology proxies such as gas fraction and stellar concentration (Lagos et al. 2017). Reviews of galaxy-formation models find a remarkable convergence between methods on a core set of processes (cosmological accretion, strong stellar-driven winds that are more efficient at low mass, and black-hole feedback that suppresses star formation at high mass), and angular momentum is the structural property that depends most directly on how that gas is accreted and removed (Somerville & Davé 2015). The measurement radius (r50 versus total), the mass range above the resolution limit and the morphological sample change j substantially, so curves from different papers are not interchangeable without checking those choices.

quenched.title: Quenched fraction
quenched.paragraph: The quenched fraction records the growth of the red sequence as a function of mass and epoch. The colour bimodality of galaxies was quantified in SDSS by Baldry et al. (2004); Peng et al. (2010) showed that the effects of stellar mass and of environment on the quiescent fraction are separable to z≈1, with mass quenching proportional to star-formation rate; Weaver et al. (2023) trace the quiescent fraction to z≈7.5; and Man & Belli (2018) review how star formation shuts off in massive galaxies, concluding that there is still no consensus on the mechanism. Simulations are tested hard on this relation because it depends on feedback. For TNG about 80% of 10^10.5 to 10^11 M☉ galaxies are quiescent at z=0 and about 50% at z=2 (Donnari et al. 2019), and the quenched fraction of massive centrals and satellites changes by up to 70% and 30% respectively with the quenching definition alone, and by up to about 50% with the SFR aperture (Donnari et al. 2021). Because those analysis choices matter as much as the physics, sim-highline stores the quenching criterion and refuses to compare different ones; most current codes quench massive galaxies with AGN feedback, which is exactly what this relation constrains.

gas.title: Cold gas fraction
gas.paragraph: The cold gas fraction gives the mass of cold gas, atomic plus molecular, per unit stellar mass. Local surveys (COLD GASS and xGASS) showed that gas fractions fall with stellar mass, that atomic fractions keep rising down to 10^9 M☉ with no plateau, and that total reservoirs stay HI-dominated across 10^9 to 10^11.5 M☉ (Saintonge et al. 2011; Catinella et al. 2018; reviewed by Saintonge & Catinella 2022). At higher redshift, star-forming galaxies contained far more molecular gas and have shorter depletion times, set by redshift and by distance from the main sequence (Tacconi et al. 2020). Simulations must post-process gas into HI and H2, which makes the relation partly a test of that step: EAGLE reproduces the observed H2 scaling relations and a rising H2 fraction toward high redshift (Lagos et al. 2015), standard-resolution EAGLE under-produces HI in galaxies below 10^10 M☉ unless the resolution is raised (Crain et al. 2017), and IllustrisTNG agrees broadly with local gas fractions (Diemer et al. 2019). Physically the relation constrains accretion, feedback and the conversion of gas to stars. In this data well the gas relation mixes several definitions (HI+H2, cold gas above a density cut, different apertures), recorded in each record's definitions.

hi-fraction.title: HI gas fraction
hi-fraction.paragraph: The HI-to-stellar mass fraction measures the atomic gas reservoir relative to the stars, and is what 21 cm surveys measure directly. xGASS finds that HI fractions keep rising with decreasing stellar mass with no plateau down to 10^9 M☉, and that total gas reservoirs stay HI-dominated (Catinella et al. 2018); the review of Saintonge & Catinella (2022) places this within the network of gas scaling relations and their links to morphology and star formation. EAGLE's reference-resolution run is HI-deficient in galaxies below 10^10 M☉ while higher-resolution runs largely are not, and at fixed stellar mass the HI content evolves strongly with redshift (Crain et al. 2017); IllustrisTNG, post-processed with a separate HI/H2 framework, agrees well with observed gas fractions at z≈0 (Diemer et al. 2019). Physically, HI traces gas that has neither been converted to molecular gas, consumed, nor expelled, so the relation constrains accretion, the neutral–molecular split, and stellar and AGN feedback. The median depends on detection limits and on the radius within which HI is summed (70 pkpc in the EAGLE work), which each record states.

h2-fraction.title: H2 gas fraction
h2-fraction.paragraph: The H2-to-stellar mass fraction is the star-forming gas reservoir relative to the stars and, with the depletion time, sets how long a galaxy can keep forming stars at its current rate. Local CO surveys (COLD GASS) found that the molecular content depends on structure, with sharp thresholds in properties such as stellar surface density (Saintonge et al. 2011); at higher redshift star-forming galaxies held much more molecular gas, with depletion times set by redshift and distance from the main sequence (Tacconi et al. 2020). In simulations H2 is assigned in post-processing, so the result depends on the prescription: Lagos et al. (2015) show that two prescriptions in EAGLE reproduce the observed scaling relations with stellar mass, SFR and surface density, with larger H2 fractions and shorter depletion times at high redshift; Diemer et al. (2019) find that TNG compares well with observations and that H2 mass correlates with SFR with an almost constant depletion time. Detection-limited samples, such as COLD GASS with M★>10^10 M☉ and CO above a limit, are not all-galaxy medians; the selection is stated in the relevant records.

btfr.title: Baryonic Tully–Fisher relation
btfr.paragraph: The baryonic Tully–Fisher relation says that the baryonic mass, stars plus gas, of a rotationally supported galaxy scales tightly with its rotation velocity, roughly as V^4. McGaugh et al. (2000) showed that the optical relation breaks for low-velocity, gas-rich galaxies but that one linear relation is restored once gas is included. With the SPARC sample, Lelli et al. (2019) find that the tightest relation uses the mean velocity along the flat part of the rotation curve, with slope 3.85±0.09 (3.5 to 4.0 allowing for systematics) and an orthogonal intrinsic scatter of only 6%. Simulations are tested on the slope and scatter because these probe feedback and halo response: NIHAO galaxies reproduce the observed inefficiency of galaxy formation through the stellar, gas and baryonic relations, with scatter of 0.08 to 0.14 dex for HI velocities of 70 to 220 km/s (Dutton et al. 2017), and EAGLE spirals show a tight mass–velocity scaling provided disk sizes satisfy constraints set by halo concentration and response (Ferrero et al. 2017). The velocity definition (flat rotation speed, line width, halo Vmax) changes the slope more than differences between models do, and several records here are zoom samples that are not volume complete. Reviews of mass estimators (Courteau et al. 2014) stress that stellar-population masses and dynamical masses each carry their own systematic uncertainties.

refs.cite: Courteau et al. 2014, Rev. Mod. Phys. 86, 47

stfr.title: Stellar-mass Tully–Fisher relation
stfr.paragraph: The stellar-mass Tully–Fisher relation is the Tully–Fisher relation with stellar mass in place of luminosity, so its slope and scatter depend on the stellar mass-to-light ratios used: Bell & de Jong (2001) showed that these vary by factors of 3 to 7 in the optical and, under a universal IMF, argued for a stellar IMF with fewer low-mass stars than Salpeter. McGaugh et al. (2000) found that the stellar relation breaks at low velocity because faint galaxies are gas dominated, which is why the baryonic version is preferred. NIHAO simulations reproduce the stellar relation with small scatter for HI velocities of 70 to 220 km/s (Dutton et al. 2017), and EAGLE spirals follow a tight mass–velocity scaling that can be reconciled with abundance matching only if disk sizes follow halo concentration and response (Ferrero et al. 2017). The relation tests the fraction of baryons locked into stars at fixed halo velocity and therefore the efficiency of feedback; because it ignores gas it is more sensitive to galaxy selection than the baryonic relation. Reviews of mass estimators (Courteau et al. 2014) stress the same point for stellar-population masses in general. The IMF assumption alone shifts the zero point by up to about 0.2 dex (Salpeter versus Chabrier).

refs.cite: Courteau et al. 2014, Rev. Mod. Phys. 86, 47

uvlf.title: UV luminosity function
uvlf.paragraph: The rest-frame UV luminosity function counts galaxies per unit comoving volume per magnitude of absolute UV magnitude. It is the most direct census of unobscured star formation at high redshift, which is why JWST analyses report it before any stellar-mass relation. It is usually fitted with a Schechter function; HST data show a smooth flattening of the faint-end slope from about -2.4 at z~10 to -1.5 at z~2 and a monotonic rise of the normalisation towards lower redshift (Bouwens et al. 2021). JWST extends the measurement to z~9-16: Harikane et al. 2023 find the star-formation rate density at z~12-16 above a constant star-formation-efficiency model, whereas Donnan et al. 2024 conclude that the evolution to z~12 can be reproduced in LCDM with younger stellar populations and no change in dust or efficiency. Simulations can be compared only after fixing the dust treatment, because intrinsic and attenuated functions differ most at the bright end: THESAN applies a dust-attenuation model and broadly matches the observed z=6-10 functions (Kannan et al. 2022), FLARES publishes dust-attenuated and intrinsic functions at z=10-15, so the JWST counts can be compared on either footing (Wilkins et al. 2023), FIRE-2 attributes the z~6 decline brighter than M1500~-20 largely to dust (Ma et al. 2018), and at the faint end the predictions follow the halo mass function and the resolution limit. Madau & Dickinson 2014 give the longer view of the star-formation history this function feeds.

sfrd.title: Cosmic star-formation rate density
sfrd.paragraph: The cosmic star-formation rate density is the star-formation rate summed over all galaxies per unit comoving volume, plotted against redshift. Observationally it rises to a peak near z~2 and declines by about an order of magnitude to the present; the standard compilation of UV and infrared surveys and its fitting function is Madau & Dickinson 2014, which assumes a Salpeter IMF. At z>8 only UV estimates exist and they depend on the dust correction and on how far down the luminosity function is integrated: Harikane et al. 2023 find a decline from z~9 to 12 and perhaps 16, and Donnan et al. 2024 confirm a gradual decline out to z~12. In simulations it is the least ambiguous quantity to extract, but it integrates over everything including galaxies below any observational limit. ASTRID shows a whole-box total and a subset above 0.3 solar masses per year that diverge at high redshift (Bird et al. 2022), THESAN runs of lower resolution lose an order of magnitude at z>10 because they miss low-mass halos (Kannan et al. 2022), and EAGLE follows the observed shape but lies below the compilation near the peak, which is why the paper also plots the curve raised by 0.2 dex (Furlong et al. 2015). Convert to a common IMF before reading offsets as physics.
